It's like with your own memory: you don't try to hold all of Wikipedia in your head. You remember the important things, write down the rest.
af-memory-systems.when:
When designing an AI assistant that needs to **remember** something across conversations:
- Support chatbot that remembers customer history
- AI assistant that remembers your preferences
- Team bot that accumulates decisions and context

If you have one-shot tasks ("translate this text") — memory isn't needed.
af-memory-systems.impact:
Without memory architecture: AI = "one-question helper". Starts from scratch every time. User is irritated: "I told you yesterday, did you forget?".

With the right architecture: AI = "colleague who remembers context". Remembers the project, work style, past decisions. Come back a week later — you continue from where you stopped.
af-memory-systems.example:
Chatbot for product managers in SaaS:

- **Short-term (in-context):** in this conversation remembers "you're currently discussing feature X"
- **External (RAG):** [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] connected to spec base and customer interviews
- **Semantic (Memory tool):** remembers "this PM works on a B2B product, prefers data-driven approach"
- **Episodic (history log):** stores specific decisions "April 3: decided to launch feature X in beta"

When PM asks "what did we decide about feature X?" — AI goes to episodic → finds the decision → answers with the date.

More in Claude: [[node:cap-memory|Memory tool]], [[node:p-files|Project Files]], [[node:i-claudemd|CLAUDE.md]].
af-memory-systems.mistakes:
Main mistake: "let's just expand the context window to a million and AI will remember everything". Expensive, slow, doesn't work in production. AI gets lost when context is too big ("lost in the middle").

Second mistake: cramming everything into one memory type. Current conversation in a RAG base — pointless, fills it with garbage. Long customer profile in every request context — overpay. Each type for its own job.

af-multimodal.title: Multimodal AI — AI that sees and hears
af-multimodal.what:
AI used to only work with text: "write an email", "translate this article". Multimodal AI handles different data types at once: text + images + audio + video.

You can show AI a screenshot of an error and ask "what's wrong here?". Or photograph an invoice and ask "put these numbers into Excel". Claude sees and reads the image, understands what's there, answers.
af-multimodal.why:
The real world isn't text. A designer shows a mockup, a marketer posts an infographic, an accountant scans a receipt. If AI only understands text — it only covers half the tasks.

Multimodal AI opens up tasks that used to require a human or specialized software: receipt reading, chart analysis, mockup understanding.
af-multimodal.when:
When the task needs more than text:
- Screenshot with error → "why isn't this working?"
- Design mockup → "build the HTML"
- Receipt photo → "extract amount and date"
- Chart from a report → "describe the trend"
- Meeting video → "short summary"

If your task is mostly text — multimodal isn't needed.
af-multimodal.impact:
Before: parsing trip receipts — a secretary spends 30 minutes typing amounts into Excel.

After: you send AI 10 receipt photos → AI extracts dates and amounts → 2 minutes for you to review.

Main point: tasks that needed "human eyes" are now done by AI.
af-multimodal.example:
Situation: someone sent you a screenshot with a Python error — a long stack trace, unclear where the problem is.

Before: you re-type the error text into AI chat (10 minutes of fiddling), then ask.

With multimodal: drop the screenshot in → "what's wrong?" → Claude sees the whole stack trace, finds the specific line: "on line 47 your `data` variable is None, but you're trying to access its attribute. Add an `if data is not None` check".

Screenshot to answer — 10 seconds.

In Claude, multimodality is [[node:cap-input-modalities|Input modalities]]: images via [[node:cap-vision|Vision]] and documents via [[node:cap-files|Files]].
af-multimodal.mistakes:
Main mistake: thinking multimodal = "AI sees everything like a human". Reality:
- Recognize objects in photos — good
- Read printed text — good
- Read handwriting — worse than specialized OCR
- Understand a busy chart with many lines — may err
- Count objects precisely in a photo — weaker

Test on your task types — don't trust generic promises.

af-fine-tuning.title: Fine-tuning vs Prompting — train or explain
af-fine-tuning.what:
Imagine you're hiring a new employee. Two options:

1. **Prompting** = give them instructions each time. "Today do it this way, tomorrow that way". Fast, flexible, you can change the approach in a minute.

2. **Fine-tuning** = "train" them for 6 months so they just know without reminders. Expensive, slow, but then works without explanation.

For 95% of tasks **prompting + examples** ([[node:pr-fewshot|few-shot]]) is enough. Fine-tuning is a last resort.
af-fine-tuning.why:
Fine-tuning sounds cool ("our own AI!"), but it's tech debt. In 3 months a new Claude version drops — better than your fine-tuned one. To use it — you fine-tune again. A quarter has passed, $10k spent, and you're still on the old model.

Prompting is instant. Change the text in the prompt — AI behavior changes. Want a new model — just switch, everything works.
af-fine-tuning.when:
Fine-tuning makes sense when:
- **Distinct style / tone** that doesn't transfer via prompt examples (rare)
- **Narrow domain** where you have THOUSANDS of input-output pairs (medicine, law)
- **You need cheaper and faster** — fine-tune a small model to replace a big one

In all other cases — prompting + RAG + tools. If you haven't tried that — don't even think about fine-tuning yet.
af-fine-tuning.impact:
The right choice saves months. Teams hear "fine-tuning" → decide it's magic → spend a quarter gathering training data → ship, it works at 80%.

At the same time another team wrote a 10-line prompt + plugged in [[node:af-rag-basics|RAG]] → they shipped at 85% in a week.

Main point: don't confuse "fashionable" with "needed".
af-fine-tuning.example:
Task: "AI answers customers in our CEO's voice — concise, friendly, no jargon".

**Try prompting first:**
```
System: Reply like our CEO. Style: concise, friendly, no corporate jargon.

Example 1: Q "when will feature X ship?" — CEO would say: "Soon. Next week. Thanks for waiting."
Example 2: Q "why is it expensive?" — CEO would say: "Because we pay people well. It's worth it."
[3-5 more examples]
```

50 prompt iterations → if it still doesn't sound like the CEO → then think fine-tuning. 80% of cases — the prompt is enough.

Claude doesn't offer fine-tuning — use [[node:prompting|Prompting]], [[node:projects|Projects]] and [[node:cap-memory|Memory]] instead.
af-fine-tuning.mistakes:
Main mistake: fine-tuning "just in case" from day one. Like tuning a car you haven't driven yet. Learn to drive first.

Second mistake: thinking fine-tuning = "AI gets smarter". No — it gets "more like your data", but may answer WORSE on questions outside that data. It's specialization, not an upgrade.

ai-native-operations.title: AI for operations teams
ai-native-operations.what:
Operations are the people who keep the company afloat: HR, finance, legal, procurement, IT. Tons of repetitive tasks: approve a vacation, categorize an invoice, update a policy, answer a routine question.

AI here doesn't make a "revolution" — it removes the routine. Frees up 2-3 hours a day per person to do what they couldn't get to before.
ai-native-operations.why:
Operations is the most "invisible" work in a company. When it works — nobody notices. When it breaks — panic. AI helps it work predictably and without heroics.

It's not about "replacing people". It's about "your team of 5 no longer has bottlenecks".
ai-native-operations.when:
When you notice:
- One person = one bottleneck ("without Mary nothing gets processed")
- Tons of routine requests distract from important work
- Policies exist but nobody remembers them — everyone asks each other
- Monday reports = 3 hours of copying into Excel
- New hires spend 2 weeks figuring out where things are
ai-native-operations.impact:
Before: HR spends 60% of time on routine questions about vacations / sick leave / certificates. After: AI answers 70% of these itself, HR works on onboarding, development, culture.

Before: finance takes 2 days for a monthly report. After: AI assembles a draft in an hour, finance spends 4 hours reviewing and analyzing.

Main point: operations people stop being "request handlers" and become strategists.
ai-native-operations.example:
5 directions inside:
- [[node:ops-process-automation|Process automation]]
- [[node:ops-decision-intelligence|Decision support via AI]]
- [[node:ops-reporting-automation|Regular reporting]]
- [[node:ops-resource-optimization|Resource optimization]]
- [[node:ops-team-workflow|Team workflows]]
ai-native-operations.mistakes:
Main mistake: try to automate everything at once. "Full AI operations transformation" — sounds great, in practice nobody uses it.

Better: pick one pain (e.g. routine HR questions) → close it with AI → see a result in 2 weeks → move to the next.

Second mistake: automating without the team's involvement. If HR didn't help configure it — they'll sabotage it. AI should be a tool operations people want to use.

ops-process-automation.title: AI Process Automation
ops-process-automation.what: Automating recurring processes via AI: input (trigger) → AI processing → output (result + next action). Skills + Hooks + RAG as the core stack.
ops-process-automation.why: Every team has 30-50% of tasks = recurring: onboarding, status updates, routine comms. AI handles most of these without quality loss.
ops-process-automation.when: When a task happens ≥5×/week + has clear inputs/outputs + result can be validated. Ideal candidates: weekly reports, customer welcome emails, internal status digests.
ops-process-automation.impact: Time savings: 70-90% on a specific task. Consistency: a single quality result instead of "depends who did it".
ops-process-automation.example:
Workflow "Weekly status digest":
1. Trigger (Monday 9am or /command).
2. AI Step: reads Linear/Jira for the week.
3. AI Step: writes executive summary in branded style.
4. Quality gate: human does final review (15 min instead of 2 hours of writing).
5. Output: publish in #leadership Slack.

Before: 2h/week. After: 15min review.
ops-process-automation.mistakes: Automating a process that has not yet "stabilized". If the process changes every week — AI automation will constantly break. First: stabilize the process manually. Then: automate.

ops-decision-intelligence.title: AI Decision Intelligence
ops-decision-intelligence.what: AI as a "second opinion" for operational decisions: AI analyzes data + context + history of decisions → gives a structured recommendation. Does not replace human, but disciplines the process.
ops-decision-intelligence.why: Operational decisions are often made "by gut" under pressure. AI structuring forces consideration of alternatives, risks, metrics — reduces reactive decisions.
ops-decision-intelligence.when: Hire/no-hire decisions. Resource allocation. Vendor selection. Process change vs no-change. Decisions with >$10k impact or >2 weeks horizon.
ops-decision-intelligence.impact: Reduction in reactive decisions: 50-70%. Decision quality measurable (track outcomes).
ops-decision-intelligence.example:
Decision template:
1. Context: situation in 5 sentences.
2. Options: 3 decision variants.
3. Each option: pros, cons, cost, risk.
4. AI analysis: pattern-matching with past decisions + recommendation.
5. Human override + log decision reasoning.

After 3 months you SEE the patterns of your decisions — where AI was right, where it erred.
ops-decision-intelligence.mistakes: Blindly following AI recommendation. AI is good at pattern analysis but does not know your full context. Treat AI as a "thoughtful junior": gives perspective, but the decision and accountability are yours.

ops-reporting-automation.title: AI Reporting Automation
ops-reporting-automation.what: Auto-generating reports from structured data: CRM, analytics, project management. AI reads data, writes insight-driven narrative, forms action items.
ops-reporting-automation.why: Teams spend 4-8 hours a week on manual reporting. AI handles 80% of the work, leaving the human with review and executive judgment.
ops-reporting-automation.when: Regular reports (weekly/monthly). Data in systems with API/export. Audience expects consistency in format. KPIs are countable.
ops-reporting-automation.impact: Time-to-report: 4 hours → 30 minutes. Before: different people, different templates. Now: one format, one tone, everywhere. Reports arrive on time, not "when I got around to it".
ops-reporting-automation.example:
Sales Weekly Report:
1. Export from CRM (HubSpot/Salesforce) → CSV.
2. Project with [[node:b-system|system prompt]]: "you are a sales analyst, report format is XYZ".
3. Prompt: "here is data for the week, write executive summary + 3 action items".
4. Output: ready report with numbers, trends, recommendations.

Metrics: reporting time 4h→30min, data accuracy 100% (autopull), insights consistency 95%.
ops-reporting-automation.mistakes: Doing "AI generates pretty text" without action. A report without action items is trash. Structure must be: what changed → why → what we do → KPI. Every time.

ops-resource-optimization.title: AI Resource Optimization
ops-resource-optimization.what: AI optimization of team resource allocation: capacity planning, tools for different tasks, Claude model choice (Haiku vs Sonnet vs Opus), API cost management.
ops-resource-optimization.why: Operations teams often overspend on tools and resources because "we have always done it this way". AI audit reveals over-provisioning, model mismatch, idle resources.
ops-resource-optimization.when: Quarterly resource review. Before annual budget planning. When AI spend becomes visible in P&L.
ops-resource-optimization.impact: Cost reduction: 20-40% on operations spend. Productivity: better tool-to-task fit.
ops-resource-optimization.example:
AI Spend Audit:
1. Export all AI-API logs for 30 days.
2. AI analysis: "which tasks use Opus, can they be moved to Sonnet?"
3. Output: list of tasks + alternative models + estimated savings.
4. Test: one week on the new mix → measure quality.
5. Roll out: if quality does not drop, move 80% of tasks.

Real case: $5k/month Opus → $1.2k/month Sonnet, quality drop <5%, ROI = 4x.
ops-resource-optimization.mistakes: Optimizing only cost without quality measurement. A cheaper model can "save" $1000 but reduce conversion by $5000. Track quality metrics in parallel with cost.

ops-team-workflow.title: AI Operations Team Workflow
ops-team-workflow.what: How an ops team orchestrates working with AI: shared prompts, shared Projects, access, knowledge management. This is about team operating model, not individual usage.
ops-team-workflow.why: Individual AI usage does not scale. A team of 10, each with their own prompting style = different results + duplicated work. Team workflow creates a unified standard.
ops-team-workflow.when: When the team ≥3 people actively use AI. When inconsistent results emerge. When a newcomer arrives and "does not know how we work with AI".
ops-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: a team of 5 does what used to take 8. New hire onboarding: 2 days instead of 2 weeks. Knowledge isn't locked "in Mary's head" — it lives in shared Projects + [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]].
ops-team-workflow.example:
Operations Team Setup:
1. Shared Claude Project "Operations Workspace" with team-style [[node:b-system|system prompt]].
2. [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] in shared repo: rules, templates, typical tasks.
3. Reusable Skills for recurring tasks (report-writer, decision-analyzer).
4. Weekly "AI office hours": team shares discoveries.
5. Metric: % of tasks done through shared workflow.

Stage 3 sign: a newcomer is productive in 2-3 days, not weeks.
ops-team-workflow.mistakes: Making "team workflow" = "one person forces everyone to use their prompts". That is not workflow, that is dictatorship. Team workflow = collaborative development + ownership + feedback loops.

ai-workflows.title: AI Workflows — how AI gets the task done step by step
ai-workflows.what:
A workflow is when you drop a file → AI parses it → you get a summary. Or: an incoming email → AI classifies → drafts a reply → you tweak → send. A workflow is a sequence of steps where AI does its part and you do yours.

Every AI tool you already use (Notion AI, Gmail Smart Reply, meeting transcribers) is a workflow. Someone just hid it behind a button.
ai-workflows.why:
When you do the same thing manually 5 times a week — that's a signal you need a workflow. Configure AI once → it works on its own from then on. You move from "open chat → copy → paste" to "press a button → get a result".

This is the difference between "playing with ChatGPT" and "I have an AI assistant that does X for me".
ai-workflows.when:
When you notice:
- You do the same action more than 3 times a week
- You copy text from one place to another
- AI helps, but every time you have to re-explain
- A team of 3+ does the same task — everyone in their own way
ai-workflows.impact:
Before: sorting email — 1 hour each morning. After: AI sorted it overnight → you spend 10 minutes in the morning checking.

Before: writing a meeting recap — 40 minutes. After: AI pulled decisions and action items from the recording → you tweak for 10 minutes.

Main point: you don't "do it faster", you "do only the important part".
ai-workflows.example:
Workflow "handle an incoming customer email" (for the pattern itself see [[node:sys-workflows-basics|What an AI Workflow really is]] and [[node:sys-linear-chain|Linear Chain]]):
1. Email arrives at support@
2. AI reads and categorizes: question / complaint / cancellation
3. If a question → AI drafts a reply based on the knowledge base
4. If a complaint → AI calls a human with a ready-made summary
5. You glance at the draft → tweak 1-2 words → send

Result: 50 emails per day instead of 15. Not because you type faster — because AI removed "start from scratch".
ai-workflows.mistakes:
Main mistake: trying to build a workflow "that does everything". Better 5 simple workflows for specific tasks than one giant one.

Second mistake: automating everything. If a step requires human judgement (important client, legal risk, money) — leave it to a human. Workflow ≠ autopilot.

ai-data-systems.title: AI Data Systems — how AI works with YOUR documents
ai-data-systems.what:
You know how Google searches websites and finds the right one? AI Data Systems is the same search, but over YOUR documents: team PDFs, Notion notes, Slack threads, CRM customer records.

Without this AI only knows what was in the internet at training time. With this — AI knows what your team knows.
ai-data-systems.why:
Without data systems AI says "I don't know" to any company-specific question. With data systems — it says "here's the doc from March 14th, it says X, here's the link".

That's the difference between "AI as Wikipedia" and "AI as a new hire who has read the entire knowledge base".
ai-data-systems.when:
When you notice:
- You ask AI about your company — it gives generic answers
- The team has a "person who remembers where things live" — a bottleneck
- New hires spend 2 weeks finding the right documents
- Customers ask the same questions — the answers exist, but they're scattered
ai-data-systems.impact:
Before: "where's our refund process?" → 30 minutes searching Notion + Slack. After: ask AI → link to doc + quote in 5 seconds.

Before: a new hire asks 20 questions in week one. After: they ask AI, only go to colleagues with genuinely complex things.

Main point: the company's knowledge stops being "in Mary's head".
ai-data-systems.example:
We connect AI to a Notion base with company policies (under the hood — [[node:sys-rag-architecture|RAG architecture]]). An employee asks in Slack: "How do I file a 5-day business trip to Berlin?"

AI:
1. Searches Notion for relevant documents (regulations, expense policy)
2. Finds 3 documents
3. Assembles the answer: "Per the 2024-03 policy (link): book flights through Concur, hotel up to €180/night, expenses within 5 days via Bookkeeper. Business trips to Germany require 7-day notice to HR."
4. Employee gets the answer in 10 seconds instead of an hour of searching
ai-data-systems.mistakes:
Main mistake: hook up "all documents" at once. You get noise — AI answers citing a 2019 draft.

Better: connect 1 source (current policies) → check answer quality → then add the rest.

Second mistake: not showing sources. If AI answers without a link to "where it got it" — nobody trusts it.

ai-native-marketing.title: AI for marketing
ai-native-marketing.what:
Marketing = content, campaigns, analytics. Always "do more, check less, deadlines were yesterday". AI here doesn't "write posts for you" — it removes the blank page: gives a first draft in a minute, you finish in your voice in 15 minutes instead of "wrote for 2 hours".

Analytics: instead of "opened 5 dashboards, merged manually" — AI reads the data and says "here's what happened this week, here's a hypothesis about why".
ai-native-marketing.why:
Marketing is always "more content, less budget, faster". AI removes the dilemma "quality vs quantity" — you can have both, if you wire it up correctly.

Main point: AI doesn't replace your brand voice. It gives you a draft in your voice, because you configured it once.
ai-native-marketing.when:
When you notice:
- Content plan exists, execution lags — no hands for drafts
- Each writer writes in their own style, brand voice is fuzzy
- Analytics is done "on Mondays when there's time" — i.e. never
- SEO — theoretically yes, in practice no time
- Campaigns planned 2 weeks ahead, launched in a week — no time to test
ai-native-marketing.impact:
Before: marketing publishes 4 posts a week. After: 12-15 posts at the same quality (AI writes drafts, marketer edits and publishes).

Before: analytics — "let's look at month-end". After: AI sends "yesterday CTR dropped 15%, likely due to creative X, recommend switching to Y" to Slack every morning.

Main point: less "writing by hand", more "deciding what to write and why".

ai-native-marketing.mistakes:
Main mistake: expecting AI to write "as you". It won't. It'll write "similar to you" — your job is to finish.

Second mistake: give the whole team ChatGPT without brand voice setup. You'll get 5 different styles in one brand's posts. First configure AI for the brand voice, then roll out to the team.

Third mistake: automating publishing. AI writes, human looks and clicks "publish" — otherwise sooner or later something embarrassing goes live.

ai-native-customer-support.title: AI for customer support
ai-native-customer-support.what:
Support = 70% routine questions ("where's my invoice", "how to change password", "email not arriving") and 30% real problems. AI closes the routine itself, agents handle only the hard stuff.

This isn't "an annoying chatbot". It's "AI that actually solves the issue in 5 seconds or calls a human if it can't".
ai-native-customer-support.why:
Support is a pain point in any product. Customer base grows → questions grow → you hire more people → budgets burn → agents burn out.

With AI, support stops scaling linearly: 100 customers = 1 agent, 10,000 customers = still 3 agents. Because AI handles 70% of routine.
ai-native-customer-support.when:
When you notice:
- Support team grows faster than customer base
- Agents write the same thing 20 times a day
- Time to first reply > 30 minutes — customers irritated
- Turnover in support — everyone burns out in 6 months
- Knowledge base exists, nobody reads it — easier to ask
ai-native-customer-support.impact:
Before: time to first reply 2 hours, agent handles 40 tickets a day.

After: AI answers routine in 5 seconds (70% of tickets), agent handles 30 complex tickets a day (but more time per one → higher quality).

Customers get answers faster, agents don't burn out on repetition, budget doesn't scale linearly with customer base.

Main point: support stops "plugging holes" and starts "helping customers succeed with the product".

ai-native-customer-support.mistakes:
Main mistake: "AI will replace support". It won't. AI closes routine, leaving the complex to humans. If you try to fully remove agents — you'll regret it after the first complaint.

Second mistake: not showing what AI says. If the agent can't see what AI told the customer — they'll duplicate, confuse, and damage the relationship. AI should be transparent to the team.

Third mistake: launching AI without escalation. Customer asks the same question 3 times, AI repeats the same answer 3 times — customer livid. You need an explicit "call a human" path.

ai-native-product.title: AI for product teams
ai-native-product.what:
A product manager spends 50% of time "gathering insights": customer interviews, feedback from support, analytics data, stakeholder tickets. And 50% on "making a decision and writing it up".

AI speeds up the first half by 5×: reads interviews, aggregates feedback, finds patterns. PM has time left for strategy.
ai-native-product.why:
Product work is "lots of noise, little signal". AI is good at separating one from the other: from 200 feedbacks it pulls out 5 real themes, from 30 interviews — 3 stable insights.

Main point: PM stops being a "feedback-tool operator" and becomes "the person who makes decisions".
ai-native-product.when:
When you notice:
- 30 customer interviews and you haven't read them yet
- 200 feedbacks from support in Notion — synthesis "someday"
- Roadmap built by "loudness", not by data
- Spending an hour every morning on "what happened in the product yesterday"
- Specs take 3 days — then a week of revisions
ai-native-product.impact:
Before: 30 customer interviews = a month of synthesis, by the end you've forgotten the first ones.

After: AI does the first-pass synthesis in 2 hours, PM verifies and digs into the important parts → 3 days instead of a month.

Before: PRD takes a week to write, a week to review.

After: AI drafts in 30 minutes from a brief, PM revises for 2 days, reviewers get a clean document.

Main point: PM works on "what's important to do", not on "how to gather data".

ai-native-product.mistakes:
Main mistake: letting AI make product decisions. AI is good at data synthesis, but "what matters more" is your job. If AI says "build X" and you build it without your own analysis — you'll blame AI when it doesn't work out.

Second mistake: automating interviews without a human. AI does the interview, AI processes it, AI decides what's important — you'll get what you already knew. Live interviews with a human are mandatory. AI speeds up processing, not replacement.

Third mistake: trusting AI "without verification". AI can hallucinate insights that aren't in the data. Always verify key conclusions against the original sources.

ai-native-enterprise.title: AI transformation for the whole company
ai-native-enterprise.what:
A section for leaders (CTO, CIO, Head of Transformation): how to roll out AI not just "in marketing" but across a 200+ person company. Strategy, change management, governance, ROI, risks.

This isn't "buy ChatGPT licenses". It's "how to make AI the way of working, not a toy in the corner".
ai-native-enterprise.why:
A big company doesn't turn AI-native in a month. It's 1-3 years of work on strategy, teams, culture and processes. Without a systematic approach — the rollout dies halfway.

This section is a map of typical transformation tasks and a warning about the rakes 80% of companies step on.
ai-native-enterprise.when:
When:
- You're a CTO/CIO at a 100+ person company and need to prepare an AI strategy
- The board asked "what's our AI story" — you need a clear answer
- You already have 5 AI pilots in different departments, but they're disconnected
- Competitors are pulling ahead — you need to catch up systematically
- You launched AI pilots — nobody uses them → need to understand why
ai-native-enterprise.impact:
Without a system: 20 pilots, 3 alive, 17 abandoned. Teams disillusioned, budget wasted.

With a system: 5 directions prioritized, 4 driven to production, measurable quarterly ROI, teams see results and want more.

Main point: AI stops being a "fashionable toy" and becomes a real way of working.

ai-native-enterprise.mistakes:
Main mistake: "push AI from the top". "Everyone now works with AI" in a CEO email — 2 weeks later everyone's back to old ways. You need bottom-up momentum from teams + top-down support.

Second mistake: measuring ROI "in 6 months". By then the project is forgotten. Measure small wins every 2-4 weeks (that's how people believe and back it).

Third mistake: not investing in training. Bought licenses, forgot the team → licenses sit idle → ROI zero. Tooling budget ≤ training budget.

en-transformation-strategy.title: AI Transformation Strategy
en-transformation-strategy.what: A document-based AI strategy for 12-24 months: vision, north-star metrics, sequencing of initiatives, investment thesis, success criteria. Not "let us use AI", but "here is HOW we win from AI".
en-transformation-strategy.why: Without explicit strategy, AI initiatives = different departments doing different things. With strategy — coordination, leverage between departments, clear priorities. Strategy doc = alignment tool for leadership.
en-transformation-strategy.when: After 6-12 months of successful pilots in several departments. When the board asks questions about AI ROI. Before annual planning. When you need to hire an AI lead.
en-transformation-strategy.impact: Decision velocity: 3× faster on AI-related decisions. Org alignment: leadership team on the same page (literally). Time-to-execution: tactical teams understand priorities in days, not months.
en-transformation-strategy.example:
AI Transformation Strategy doc (8-12 pages):

1. Vision (1 page): where the company is in 2 years with AI
2. North-star metrics (3-5): cost reduction, revenue growth, NPS, talent retention
3. Strategic bets (3-7): "Stage-by-stage AI in customer support", "AI-augmented product development", ...
4. Sequencing: what we do Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4
5. Investment thesis: where we spend, where we save
6. Risk & governance principles
7. Success criteria + checkpoints

Creation process: 2-3 weeks with executives + tactical leads. Reviewed quarterly.

Metric: % of strategic decisions referencing the doc (target: >80% in 6 months).
en-transformation-strategy.mistakes: Making a strategy doc "once and forgotten". The AI landscape changes every 6 months — the strategy must refresh quarterly. And: not making just vision without metrics. Strategy without measurable outcomes = wish list.

en-change-management.title: AI Change Management
en-change-management.what: Structured approach to changing team behaviors under AI-native operations: communication, training, role evolution, resistance management. Tech adoption ≠ change management — these are different disciplines.
en-change-management.why: The most common cause of failed AI initiatives is not tech, but adoption. Teams fear (job loss), do not believe (saw hype before), do not know (skills gap). Change management addresses this explicitly.
en-change-management.when: Before rolling out a tactical direction to the full team. When the first pilots work but adoption stalls. When there is an "AI champions" vs "AI skeptics" split on the team.
en-change-management.impact: Adoption rate: 30% → 80% with proper change mgmt. Resistance reduced (not eliminated). Skills gap closes via structured training. Time-to-Stage 3: -50% for tactical directions.
en-change-management.example:
Change Management Framework (for one tactical direction):

Phase 1: Awareness (week 1-2)
  - All-hands: "here is what we are doing + why"
  - Q&A sessions: address concerns openly
  - Champions identification

Phase 2: Education (week 3-4)
  - Hands-on workshops for everyone
  - Skill development: 10 hours of structured learning
  - Champions trained deeper

Phase 3: Adoption (week 5-12)
  - Pilot teams using daily
  - Office hours for help
  - Wins shared widely

Phase 4: Reinforcement (ongoing)
  - Promotion criteria include AI usage
  - Career path for "AI-augmented" roles
  - Continuous learning culture

Metric: % of team actively using AI weekly.
en-change-management.mistakes: Thinking that training = change management. Training is skill transfer. Change mgmt is behavioral shift. Without the second, the first = waste. And: not answering "will I lose my job?". Avoiding it = doubt grows.

en-governance.title: AI Governance
en-governance.what: Set of rules and processes governing how AI is used in the organization: data privacy, model selection, output validation, vendor management, compliance. Not "security team forbids" — but "structured framework for responsible use".
en-governance.why: Without governance, compliance gaps accumulate: data leaks via AI inputs, customer data in third-party models, audit trail missing. Regulatory landscape (GDPR, EU AI Act) tightens — better get ahead.
en-governance.when: Before production AI use cases (NOT after). When there is customer data, financial data, PII in AI flows. When multiple departments use different AI tools.
en-governance.impact: Compliance: prevented incidents. Trust: customers trust AI products. Speed: clear rules speed up decision-making (no "can we or can we not?" discussions). Risk reduction quantifiable.
en-governance.example:
AI Governance Framework:

1. Data classification: what can/cannot go into AI flows
   - Public data: any AI tool
   - Internal data: approved enterprise tools only
   - Customer data: with consent + data residency check
   - PII: encrypted + DPA in place

2. Vendor management:
   - Approved AI tools list (updated quarterly)
   - DPA requirements
   - Audit logs

3. Output validation:
   - Human review for customer-facing AI outputs
   - Quality monitoring (statistical)
   - Bias testing

4. Incident response:
   - AI-specific incident playbook
   - Reporting channels

Reviewed: quarterly + after any incident.

Metric: incidents per quarter (target: 0 high-severity).
en-governance.mistakes: Doing governance as a "list of prohibitions". Governance works as an enabler if framed as "here is how to do this responsibly". Without enablement framing — shadow AI usage (teams use unauthorized tools).

en-coe.title: AI Center of Excellence
en-coe.what: Central team (3-10 people) — AI lead, ML engineers, AI ethicists, product manager — supporting tactical teams: best practices, shared infrastructure, training, governance liaison. Not building everything, but enabling others.
en-coe.why: Without a CoE, each tactical team reinvents the wheel: discovers RAG, learns prompt engineering, sets up vector DB. CoE shares this knowledge and infrastructure → 5-10× faster for all subsequent teams.
en-coe.when: After 2-3 successful tactical AI directions. When "how and where do I find an AI expert?" becomes a regular question. When signing up for enterprise AI vendors (CoE manages).
en-coe.impact: New AI initiative time-to-launch: 6 months → 2 months. Cost: shared infra cheaper than per-team setup. Quality: best practices spread. Career: clear AI path for talent.
en-coe.example:
CoE Structure:

Core team (3-5):
  - Head of AI / Chief AI Officer
  - Senior ML/AI engineer
  - AI Product Manager
  - AI Ethics & Governance lead

Functions:
  1. Shared infrastructure (vector DBs, LLM API contracts, monitoring)
  2. Best practices library ([[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] templates, Skills, patterns)
  3. Office hours (weekly, anyone can attend)
  4. Training programs (3 levels: foundational, intermediate, advanced)
  5. Tooling decisions (which AI tools company-wide)
  6. Governance coordination (with security/legal)
  7. Talent: hiring AI roles + upskilling existing
  8. Showcase: monthly "AI demos" across the company

Key metric: CoE-enabled launches per quarter.
en-coe.mistakes: Making CoE "the AI department" — building everything. CoE = enablement, not execution. Tactical teams build, CoE shares know-how. Otherwise CoE becomes a bottleneck.

en-roi-measurement.title: AI ROI Measurement
en-roi-measurement.what: Framework for measuring AI investment returns: cost vs value, attribution to AI vs other factors, leading vs lagging indicators, payback period. Turns "AI saves time" into "AI saved $X this quarter".
en-roi-measurement.why: Without ROI measurement, AI initiatives ride on vibes. When finance asks "show me the money?", the response should be quantified. ROI measurement = sustainable AI program longevity.
en-roi-measurement.when: After 3-6 months of AI in production. Before budget planning (annual or quarterly). When executives ask about AI value. When you need to prioritize between AI initiatives.
en-roi-measurement.impact: Budget approval: 2× faster for AI initiatives with tracked ROI. Resource allocation: efficient (kill failing, double on winning). Stakeholder confidence: high.
en-roi-measurement.example:
AI ROI Framework:

Cost side:
  - Direct: AI API costs, tools, infrastructure
  - Indirect: training time, change management, governance overhead
  - Hidden: opportunity cost of team time

Value side:
  - Time saved (× hourly cost of saved roles)
  - Quality improvement (cost of errors avoided)
  - Revenue generated (new capabilities)
  - Risk reduction (compliance, incidents avoided)
  - Customer satisfaction (retention impact)

Attribution: how to know AI caused this?
  - Before/after comparison + control group when possible
  - A/B testing on features
  - Counterfactual analysis for high-stakes claims

Reporting:
  - Monthly per tactical direction
  - Quarterly aggregate to leadership
  - Annual: full impact report

Metric: documented ROI per initiative > 3× cost (target).
en-roi-measurement.mistakes: Counting only cost savings, ignoring intangibles. AI brings not only time — but capability gains, morale, future optionality. Without holistic ROI — value undervalued, program cancelled prematurely.

en-risk-management.title: AI Risk Management
en-risk-management.what: Systematic identification, assessment, mitigation of AI-specific risks: hallucinations in production, model drift, data leaks, regulatory non-compliance, bias, vendor dependencies. Risk awareness, not risk avoidance.
en-risk-management.why: AI risks differ from traditional IT risks: probabilistic, evolving, often invisible until late. Traditional risk frameworks do not catch them. Need an AI-specific approach.
en-risk-management.when: From day 1 of every AI initiative (NOT after an incident). Before production launch. Annually for existing AI systems. After any notable industry incident.
en-risk-management.impact: High-severity incidents: 0 prevented to occurred (best outcome). Insurance cost: lower with documented program. Regulatory readiness: ahead of EU AI Act, NIST framework.
en-risk-management.example:
AI Risk Categories + Mitigations:

1. Hallucinations:
   - Risk: AI returns wrong info confidently
   - Mitigation: RAG with citations, human review for customer-facing, quality monitoring

2. Model drift:
   - Risk: AI behavior changes without notice (model update, data shift)
   - Mitigation: continuous quality monitoring, golden test sets, rollback ability

3. Data leaks:
   - Risk: customer/sensitive data in model providers
   - Mitigation: data classification, approved vendors, encryption, audit logs

4. Bias:
   - Risk: AI discriminates (hiring, pricing, content)
   - Mitigation: bias testing, diverse training data, monitoring by demographic

5. Regulatory:
   - Risk: GDPR, EU AI Act, sector-specific violations
   - Mitigation: compliance review per use case, legal sign-off, documentation

6. Vendor lock:
   - Risk: depends entirely on one AI provider
   - Mitigation: abstraction layer, multi-vendor strategy, internal fallback

Risk register: updated quarterly.

Metric: identified vs occurred risks (catch rate target: >90%).
en-risk-management.mistakes: Thinking risk management = compliance checklist. Real AI risk management = thinking about edge cases, scenarios, second-order effects. Checklist alone — false security.

en-talent-strategy.title: AI Talent Strategy
en-talent-strategy.what: Approach to building AI capability on the team: hiring AI roles, upskilling existing employees, retention in the AI-talent market, career paths for AI-augmented roles. Talent is the hardest part for long-term AI success.
en-talent-strategy.why: AI tools are commodity, AI talent is not. Companies without a talent strategy lose people to Big Tech. Companies with a good strategy attract top talent, retain existing employees via growth opportunities.
en-talent-strategy.when: Continuously (not "one time"). Before every tactical direction launch. When scaling the AI program. When attrition in AI-relevant roles rises.
en-talent-strategy.impact: AI talent retention: 90%+ (vs 60% industry average). Time-to-fill AI roles: 2× faster (employer brand). Internal mobility: 30%+ move into AI-augmented roles.
en-talent-strategy.example:
AI Talent Strategy:

1. Hiring framework:
   - Roles needed: ML engineers, AI PMs, AI ethicists, prompt engineers
   - Compensation benchmarks (AI talent premium)
   - Sourcing channels (universities, conferences, community)

2. Upskilling:
   - 3 levels: foundational (everyone), intermediate (heavy users), advanced (builders)
   - Time budget: 4-8 hours/month protected learning time
   - Recognition: AI skills in performance reviews

3. Career paths:
   - "AI-augmented" version of every role (e.g., AI-augmented PM, AI-augmented designer)
   - New roles: AI ops, AI product, prompt engineer
   - Senior path for AI builders

4. Retention:
   - AI projects = career capital (assignment to AI work seen as opportunity)
   - Internal mobility: skill-based moves to AI-heavy teams
   - External brand: conference talks, blog posts, GitHub

5. Culture:
   - "AI-curious" as core value
   - Failed AI experiments celebrated (learning culture)
   - Cross-team AI showcases

Metric: AI skills inventory (% of workforce with documented AI proficiency).
en-talent-strategy.mistakes: Hiring ML engineers and thinking talent strategy is done. They build, but do not replace product, marketing, support skill needs. AI talent strategy = broad upskilling + targeted hiring. Not one or the other.

ai-orchestration.title: A team of multiple AIs
ai-orchestration.what:
Sometimes one AI isn't enough. The task is too big, requires different skills, needs steps that depend on each other. Then you build an AI team: one writes, another checks, a third decides what to do next.

Like a real team: each AI has its own role, they hand work over to each other, and you watch from the outside.
ai-orchestration.why:
One AI in a complex task is like asking a single person to be a copywriter, editor, fact-checker and lawyer at the same time. They can do all of it — but poorly.

A team of AIs lets each one focus on its piece. Output quality jumps not because the model is smarter, but because each role is set up properly.
ai-orchestration.when:
When you notice:
- One AI handles a task at 70% quality — there's a ceiling
- The task has clear stages with different skills (research → writing → fact-check → polish)
- You want repeatable quality without retrying 5 times
- A single prompt has turned into a wall of text with 20 rules — impossible to maintain (for base patterns see [[node:sys-multi-agent-patterns|Multi-Agent — 4 ways]])
ai-orchestration.impact:
One AI: 70% acceptable outputs.

Team of AIs: 90% acceptable outputs. Not because the model improved, but because each step has clear focus.

Main point: instead of fighting one prompt that does it all, you assemble a team where each member does one thing well.
ai-orchestration.example:
Writing analytical articles:
1. **Researcher AI**: takes the topic, finds 10 sources, makes a summary with facts and quotes
2. **Outline AI**: takes the research, builds an article structure (intro, 3 blocks, conclusion)
3. **Writer AI**: takes the outline, writes the first draft in the brand voice
4. **Fact-checker AI**: takes the draft, checks every claim against sources, marks doubtful ones
5. **Editor AI**: removes water, tightens long sentences
6. Person: reads, makes final edits, publishes

Result: 1 hour of work instead of a day. Each step is debuggable separately.
ai-orchestration.mistakes:
Main mistake: build a team of AIs for a simple task. If one AI handles it well — don't complicate.

Second mistake: not setting clear interfaces between AIs. "AI 1 gives some text, AI 2 figures out what to do with it" = chaos. Each step needs a clear input and output format.

Third mistake: not adding humans in the right places. A fully autonomous team of AIs without checkpoints will drift in unexpected directions in 2 weeks.

ai-human-collaboration.title: AI + Human — who does what
ai-human-collaboration.what:
The border between "AI does it itself" and "calls a human". Worried AI will send something dumb to a client? Or the opposite — that every action will require your approval and you'll sit there as an operator?

AI-Human Collaboration is about where to draw that line: what AI does itself, what it shows you for review, what it doesn't touch at all.
ai-human-collaboration.why:
Without an explicit line, AI is either too cautious (calls a human for everything — annoying) or too autonomous (sent something weird to a client — embarrassing).

The right line: AI does 70% of tasks itself, 25% shows a draft to a human, 5% doesn't touch at all.
ai-human-collaboration.when:
When you're wondering:
- Can we trust AI to send client emails without review?
- What if AI gets a financial report wrong?
- Where's the line between "assistant" and "autopilot"?
- The team is afraid to give AI more permissions, but reviewing everything manually doesn't scale
ai-human-collaboration.impact:
A well-tuned border: AI works fast and autonomously where it's safe, humans step in where it matters.

Wrong: either "AI sent rubbish to a client — shut it down" or "AI asks for approval 200 times a day — turned off because it's annoying".

Main point: people work on hard things, AI works on the repetitive ones.
ai-human-collaboration.example:
Customer support at a SaaS startup:
- AI answers "how to change password", "where to download an invoice", "when does my plan renew" on its own — 70% of tickets
- AI drafts a reply and shows a human for "bug complaint", "refund question" — 25%
- AI doesn't touch "legal claims", "major accounts", "security" — 5% goes straight to a senior (mechanics — see [[node:sys-escalation-paths|Escalation: when AI calls a human]])

Result: a team of 3 handles what used to need 8.
ai-human-collaboration.mistakes:
Main mistake: "let AI write drafts for now, we'll review everything". A week later the team is burned out reviewing identical drafts and starts sending without looking. Better: explicitly say "these 5 ticket types AI handles itself, these 3 — for review".

Second mistake: setting a threshold by AI confidence ("if confidence > 80% — send"). AI is always confident. Set the border by task type, not by "model confidence".

ai-operations.title: AI in production — so it doesn't break in a month
ai-operations.what:
You shipped an AI feature → it works → 2 weeks later quality drops → users complain → you don't know why. AI Operations is a set of practices to prevent that.

It includes: watching what AI actually replies (instead of trusting "it's fine"), measuring quality regularly, controlling how much you spend on the API, versioning prompts like code.
ai-operations.why:
AI doesn't behave like regular software. Regular code: wrote it → works → works. AI code: wrote it → works → a month later the model is updated → behaves differently.

Without AI Ops your AI = an eternal pilot. With AI Ops — a production system that lives for years.
ai-operations.when:
From day one in production. Not "when we need to" — by then it's too late.

Signals you're missing Ops:
- You don't know how much you spent on AI last month
- Users complain about quality — you can't verify if it actually got worse
- The prompt was changed 5 times — you don't remember which version is in prod
- AI started answering oddly — you don't know if the model was updated or the prompt was edited
ai-operations.impact:
Without Ops: an AI feature lives 3 months, then "something broke", the team gets tired of fixing it → they kill it.

With Ops: an AI feature lives 2+ years, you spot degradation in a day instead of a month, costs are predictable.

Main point: you run the system, not the other way around.
ai-operations.example:
AI support chat in a B2B SaaS:
1. Every week 50 typical questions are auto-run (see [[node:sys-evals-benchmarks|How to actually check AI works]]) → answer quality checked → if it drops 10%, alert
2. A daily Slack report: "yesterday 340 requests, $4.20 spent, 92% positive feedback"
3. All prompts live in git, costs under control (see [[node:sys-cost-management|How not to go broke on the AI API]]), changes need review from 2 people
4. If AI starts answering 30% longer than usual → automatic alert (often a sign of degradation)

The team catches issues in a day, not a customer complaint two weeks later.
ai-operations.mistakes:
Main mistake: "we'll launch first, think about monitoring later". A month in you have 10,000 requests and zero data about what AI said. You can't even tell if quality got worse.

Second mistake: measuring only "works / doesn't work". You need to measure quality — otherwise you'll miss slow degradation where AI answers technically correctly but not what's needed.

ai-integration-systems.title: AI inside the tools you already use
ai-integration-systems.what:
AI in Slack, where you already chat. AI in Notion, where your docs live. AI in Linear, where the tickets are. Integration means AI comes to your tools, not the other way around.

The opposite: "open ChatGPT → copy context → paste → copy the answer → paste back". Nobody keeps doing that for long.
ai-integration-systems.why:
AI without integration = a cool demo that nobody uses. Because switching between Slack and ChatGPT and back is exhausting.

AI inside the tool that's already open = used every day, no reminders needed.
ai-integration-systems.when:
When you notice:
- You shipped an AI tool → the team is impressed → 2 weeks later nobody opens it
- People say "cool, but I forget it exists"
- Most of the team's work lives in Slack / Notion / Linear / CRM
- AI = a separate tab people close first
ai-integration-systems.impact:
AI in chat: 10-20% of the team uses it.
AI inside Slack/Notion: 60-80% use it.

Not because it works better — because there's no need to go anywhere.

Main point: AI becomes part of the workflow, not a separate step.
ai-integration-systems.example:
A sales team works in HubSpot (under the hood — [[node:sys-api-patterns|API integration patterns]]). Before:
1. Rep sees an email from a customer
2. Goes to ChatGPT
3. Copies the conversation history
4. Asks "write a follow-up"
5. Copies the result back to HubSpot

Now:
1. Rep sees the email in HubSpot
2. Clicks "AI follow-up" right in the card
3. AI already knows the customer's history, recent deals, tone of voice
4. Gets 3 draft options
5. Picks one → tweaks → sends

From 5 minutes to 30 seconds. But more importantly — the rep actually does it, instead of "forgetting about AI".
ai-integration-systems.mistakes:
Main mistake: build a "portal" — a separate website where all AI features live. Nobody goes there. Better to embed AI into 1 tool the team uses daily.

Second mistake: integrate AI everywhere at once. You'll get 10 half-baked integrations. Better 1 integration that actually works (Slack or Notion or CRM — pick one).

ai-native-design.title: AI for design teams
ai-native-design.what:
Design = "do 5 interviews → synthesize → sketch 10 prototypes → gather feedback → redo". Many steps, each slow.

AI speeds up everything between "the research is done" and "the final mockup": synthesizes interviews, generates prototype ideas, checks accessibility, supports the design system, writes UX copy.
ai-native-design.why:
A designer spends 60% of time on "prep work": organizing research, routine edits, consistency checks. AI removes the routine — the designer focuses on creativity and strategy.

Main point: AI doesn't "draw for you". It speeds up everything around drawing so you have more time to think.
ai-native-design.when:
When you notice:
- 10 user interviews sit in Notion, you synthesized two
- Every week you check by hand that mockups have alt text
- A design system exists but everyone draws their own way
- UX copy is written by the product writer, you wait 2 days
- "Prototype variants" eat 3 days, you end up picking the first one
ai-native-design.impact:
Before: synthesizing 10 interviews = a week.

After: AI does the first-pass synthesis in 2 hours, designer verifies and finalizes → 1-2 days.

Before: 3 prototype variants in a day — not enough time.

After: AI generates 10 idea variants in an hour, designer picks 3 and goes deep.

Main point: more time on "deciding what's better", less on "gathering material".
ai-native-design.example:
7 directions inside:
- [[node:ds-design-research|Research synthesis — working with interviews]]
- [[node:ds-prototype-generation|Prototype idea generation]]
- [[node:ds-design-ops|Design ops automation]]
- [[node:ds-accessibility|Accessibility audits]]
- [[node:ds-design-system|Design system evolution]]
- [[node:ds-content-design|Content / UX copy]]
- [[node:ds-team-workflow|Team workflows]]
ai-native-design.mistakes:
Main mistake: expecting AI to "come up with the design for you". It won't. AI gives variants — your job is to pick and refine.

Second mistake: using AI for final mockups. AI is good at sketches and drafts. On final mockups your hand and taste decide.

Third mistake: automating design review. "AI will check the design for consistency" — won't replace design review with the team. Use AI for mechanical checks (alt text, contrast), but design judgement — on humans.

ds-design-research.title: AI Design Research
ds-design-research.what: AI-powered user research for designers: synthesis of usability tests, behavioral analysis of session recordings, competitor design pattern analysis. From "100 interviews = 2 weeks of processing" — to "AI extracts themes in an hour, designer validates".
ds-design-research.why: Research is a critical part of design, but time-intensive. The designer spends 50% of time on synthesis, 50% on actual design. AI shifts the balance to 20/80.
ds-design-research.when: Usability testing rounds (5-15 sessions). Competitor research. Card sorting analysis. When there are session recordings and you need to extract patterns.
ds-design-research.impact: Time-to-insight: days → hours. Theme extraction structured instead of "designer's gut feel".
ds-design-research.example:
Usability Synthesis Workflow:

  Inputs:
  - 10 session recordings (transcripts)
  - User interview notes
  - Pre/post task survey data
        ↓
  AI Steps:
  1. Extract pain points (frequency + severity)
  2. Group by user task / journey stage
  3. Identify quick wins vs structural issues
  4. Generate improvement hypotheses
        ↓
  Designer validates:
  - Pain point severity rated through design lens
  - Solutions ranked by feasibility
        ↓
  Output: structured research report + prioritized backlog

Metric: time-to-insight, design improvements shipped.
ds-design-research.mistakes: Doing AI synthesis without designer eye-on-data. AI misses emotional nuance, frustration patterns, edge cases. Workflow: AI extracts themes → designer reviews 20% with original recordings → confidence in the rest.

ds-prototype-generation.title: AI Prototype Generation
ds-prototype-generation.what: AI generation of prototypes: design mockup → HTML/React code, sketches → Figma compositions, multiple style variants in minutes. From "designer codes prototype for 2 days" — to "AI provides 5 variants in an hour, designer selects + refines".
ds-prototype-generation.why: Prototyping is a bottleneck in the design cycle. AI handles the "technical" aspect (turn idea into code/Figma), the designer focuses on concept + critique.
ds-prototype-generation.when: Early-stage exploration (need many variants quickly). Design system component variants. Conversion of mockup to code. A/B testing variant generation.
ds-prototype-generation.impact: Time-to-prototype: 2 days → 4 hours. Variant coverage: 1-2 → 5-10 per concept. Iteration speed: 2-3× faster.
ds-prototype-generation.example:
Prototype Workflow:

  Designer brief:
  "Onboarding flow for B2B SaaS,
   3 steps, brand color #2563eb,
   font Inter, mood: friendly+confident"
        ↓
  AI Step 1: Generate 5 layout variants
        ↓
  Designer selects 2 most promising
        ↓
  AI Step 2: Generate React/HTML for each
        ↓
  Designer refines via Figma OR direct code edits
        ↓
  Output: working prototype 4 hours after brief

Real usage: AI-generated code = starting point, not final. Designer refines 30-50%.
ds-prototype-generation.mistakes: Expecting "pixel-perfect output" from AI. AI gives 70% from idea to code, the last 30% (taste, brand fit, accessibility) — designer. Treating AI as starting point = speed. Treating as final = mediocre output.

ds-design-ops.title: AI Design Operations
ds-design-ops.what: Automating design ops: asset documentation, component change-logs, Figma library management, design QA. From "we have everything but no one knows where" — to "AI maintains documentation continuously".
ds-design-ops.why: Design ops are invisible until they break. Asset chaos, outdated components, missing docs — all kill velocity. AI maintains this continuously without manual effort.
ds-design-ops.when: Design system exists but is poorly documented. Multiple designers, components diverge. New hires ask "where is X component?". Pre-handoff QA is not performed.
ds-design-ops.impact: Designer time on ops: -50%. New hire onboarding: 2 weeks → 1 week. Component reuse: +30% (instead of reinvention).
ds-design-ops.example:
Design Ops Automation:

1. Component Documentation:
   - AI reads Figma file → generates MD docs per component
   - Updates: AI diffs changes weekly → adds changelog

2. Asset Audit:
   - AI scans products → finds inconsistent components
   - Flags: "button styles diverge across 5 screens"

3. Handoff QA:
   - Pre-handoff AI checks: token usage, accessibility, spacing
   - Generates QA report for dev review

4. Library Health:
   - Weekly: AI identifies unused components, outdated tokens
   - Suggests cleanup

Metric: design system health score, time saved on documentation.
ds-design-ops.mistakes: Doing AI design ops without integration into actual tools. "AI generates docs in a separate Notion" = no one reads. AI must live where designers work: Figma plugins, Slack integrations, CI/CD for design.

ds-accessibility.title: AI Accessibility Automation
ds-accessibility.what: AI a11y checks at every step: contrast checks, alt-text generation, screen reader simulation, keyboard navigation audit. From "accessibility = a special audit once every six months" — to "accessibility-by-default through AI".
ds-accessibility.why: Accessibility is often checked at the end, when fixing is expensive. AI catches issues in real-time during design. Cost is 10× lower.
ds-accessibility.when: Design system accessibility setup. New feature launches with user-facing UI. Quarterly product audits. Customer complaints about a11y issues.
ds-accessibility.impact: A11y bug rate: 30% → 5% (issues caught at design stage). Compliance: WCAG AA reached confidently. Legal risk: significantly reduced.
ds-accessibility.example:
A11y Automation Pipeline:

  Design phase:
  1. AI checks contrast ratios on every screen
  2. Auto-generates alt-text suggestions for images
  3. Flags missing focus states, keyboard traps
  4. Reviews color usage (color as sole indicator?)

  Pre-handoff:
  5. Full WCAG checklist auto-run
  6. Report: issues + recommendations + WCAG criteria mapping

  Post-launch:
  7. Real screen reader test simulation
  8. AI describes UX as a blind user would experience it

Metric: WCAG compliance %, a11y issues per release.
ds-accessibility.mistakes: Thinking AI = "full a11y replacement". Manual testing with real assistive tech (real screen readers, real keyboard navigation) — still required. AI catches 80%, the last 20% — manual + user testing with a11y users.

ds-design-system.title: AI Design System Evolution
ds-design-system.what: AI helps evolve the design system: token set generation, component variants, documentation for every component, usage migration on breaking changes. Design system from a "static document" to "a living system with an AI helper".
ds-design-system.why: Design systems usually stagnate: no resources for maintenance, breaking changes are postponed. AI removes the operational burden — the system stays fresh.
ds-design-system.when: Design system exists but maintenance burden is high. Migration to a new token system. Component variants need to be created (sizes, states, themes). Documentation is scattered across different places.
ds-design-system.impact: Design system update velocity: 3-5× faster. Migration speed: weeks → days. Documentation freshness: always current.
ds-design-system.example:
Design System Evolution:

1. Token Generation:
   - Designer says "brand uses warm palette, modern feel"
   - AI generates: color scale, spacing scale, typography scale
   - Designer refines: 70% AI output → 30% manual adjustment

2. Component Variants:
   - Designer creates base button
   - AI generates: sizes (sm/md/lg), states (default/hover/focus/disabled), themes (light/dark)
   - Outputs Figma file + code stubs

3. Breaking Change Migration:
   - "We changed token spacing from 4px to 8px"
   - AI scans codebase + Figma files
   - Generates migration PR + Figma changes list

4. Documentation:
   - AI maintains MDX docs per component
   - Updates on component changes automatically

Metric: components shipped, time-to-update.
ds-design-system.mistakes: Relying entirely on AI for design system decisions. The design system embodies brand strategy + UX principles — these are critical human decisions. AI = executor, not decision-maker for system architecture.

ds-content-design.title: AI Content Design
ds-content-design.what: AI help with UX writing: microcopy for buttons/forms/errors, onboarding flows, empty states, helper text. From "designer writes copy in free time" — to "AI generates contextual copy, designer curates voice".
ds-content-design.why: UX copy is critical for UX, but designer time on copy is always insufficient. AI generates options, the designer chooses + refines by brand voice.
ds-content-design.when: New feature launches with substantial UI text. Onboarding flow design. Error message standardization. International product (multiple languages).
ds-content-design.impact: Copy generation time: -70%. Coverage: 100% of UI elements have intentional copy (vs "TBD"). Consistency: brand voice maintained across the product.
ds-content-design.example:
Content Design Workflow:

For each UI surface:
  1. Designer provides context: "password reset flow, friendly tone"
  2. AI generates 5 variants for each microcopy slot:
     - Page title
     - Description (1 sentence)
     - Primary CTA
     - Error states (3-5 likely errors)
     - Success state
  3. Designer picks the best + may refine
  4. AI suggests improvements based on brand voice
  5. Final copy documented in content style guide

For i18n:
  - AI does first-pass translation
  - Local copywriter refines (we still need humans here)

Metric: copy coverage %, brand voice consistency score.
ds-content-design.mistakes: Using AI for legal/compliance copy without review. "AI wrote it" does not release from accountability. Critical copy (privacy notices, ToS, regulatory text) — human-written, AI only for review.

ds-team-workflow.title: AI Design Team Workflow
ds-team-workflow.what: Design team operating model with AI: shared Figma plugins, design system AI helpers, weekly "AI office hours" for designers, AI-aware critique sessions. From "every designer with their own Claude" — to a "design-augmented team".
ds-team-workflow.why: Individual designer AI usage does not scale — voice is inconsistent, components diverge, lessons are not learned. Team workflow consolidates AI value.
ds-team-workflow.when: Design team ≥3 designers actively use AI. When the product is design-driven (consumer apps, brand-heavy). When inconsistent AI usage causes brand fragmentation.
ds-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: +25-35%. Brand consistency: significantly improved. Designer career growth: "AI-augmented designer" as senior path.
ds-team-workflow.example:
Design Team Setup:

1. Shared Claude Project "Design Workspace":
   - Brand voice guide indexed
   - Design system docs accessible
   - Past research synthesized
   - Component library reference

2. [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]: design principles, brand voice, accessibility rules.

3. Skills (Figma plugins + Claude):
   - microcopy-generator
   - component-doc-writer
   - accessibility-checker
   - research-synthesizer

4. Weekly rituals:
   - "AI office hours" (30 min): designers share wins/failures
   - Quarterly "AI in design" retrospective

5. Critique enhancements:
   - Pre-critique: AI runs accessibility/brand checks
   - Critique focuses on craft + concept (not finding bugs)

Stage 3 sign: new designer productive in 3-5 days.
ds-team-workflow.mistakes: Making "AI in design" = "designer is required to use AI". Forced adoption kills creative ownership. AI must be "discovered through value" — designers choose to use it when it makes them better, faster, happier.

ai-native-ecommerce.title: AI for eCommerce
ai-native-ecommerce.what:
Flagship transformation direction: how AI changes how catalog, merchandising, CRO, support, and analytics teams work in an online store. 15 nodes with explicit workflows, metrics, and links to Foundation/Systems.

This isn't "AI recommendations" in the abstract — it's concrete scenarios: "10k SKUs with no descriptions → AI generates PDPs in minutes", "site search returns nothing → semantic search via embeddings", "CRO tests take 6 weeks → AI generates variants in an hour".
ai-native-ecommerce.why:
E-commerce is the clearest vertical market for AI: processes are documented, metrics are measurable, ROI is measurable directly (revenue, conversion, AOV). This makes the domain the best ground for systematic AI adoption.

The key: AI here isn't cosmetic — it replaces existing manual processes. PDP copywriters, merchandisers, analysts — all get 5-10× leverage from AI at the same headcount.
ai-native-ecommerce.when: When the catalog has >500 SKUs and the content team is ≤5. When conversion has plateaued for 3-6 months. When search returns "no results" >20% of the time. When merchandising is manual and goes stale within a day. When the service team is drowning in routine queries. When entering a new market and localization is needed.
ai-native-ecommerce.impact:
Across the whole direction the expected shifts: PDP time-to-publish 4h → 5min, search conversion +20-40%, average recommendation quality +30%, support load −50% on tier-1, time-to-insight on data days → hours.

Key point — measurability: every rollout can be counted in revenue within 90 days.
ai-native-ecommerce.example:
15 nodes in the direction, grouped by value stream:

**Catalog:** [[node:ec-pdp-gen|AI PDP Generation]], [[node:ec-search-opt|AI Search]], [[node:ec-merchandising|AI Merchandising]], [[node:ec-recommendations|AI Recommendations]]

**Conversion:** [[node:ec-cro|AI CRO]], [[node:ec-experimentation|AI Experimentation]], [[node:ec-checkout-opt|AI Checkout Optimization]], [[node:ec-personalization|AI Personalization]]

**Operations:** [[node:ec-support|AI Commerce Support]], [[node:ec-loyalty|AI Loyalty]], [[node:ec-analytics|AI Analytics]], [[node:ec-pricing|AI Pricing]], [[node:ec-inventory|AI Inventory]], [[node:ec-segmentation|AI Segmentation]]

**Team:** [[node:ec-team-workflow|Team Workflow]]
ai-native-ecommerce.mistakes:
The main mistake — trying "everything at once". 15 nodes = a map of possibilities, not an adoption roadmap. Start with one node, give it 60-90 days, count ROI, then expand.

Second mistake: AI generation with no quality gate. On a 10k SKU catalog a badly tuned AI will produce 10k bad cards in an hour — worse than 100 good manual ones. A quality gate is mandatory.

Third: not localizing brand voice. Generic AI-English on a Finnish or Russian market is spotted by shoppers instantly.
